subject: forensic-medicine
title: Tandem Bullets, Dumdum Bullets and Blast Injuries

steps.title: Tandem bullet, two through one hole
steps.tx: More bullets inside the body than entrance wounds on it defines the **tandem or piggyback bullet**. A faulty weapon or old ammunition left loaded for years in heat and humidity fires weakly, and the first bullet lodges in the barrel. The next shot drives it out, carrying the stuck bullet ahead, and both enter through a single entrance wound. They may separate inside the body or before reaching the target.
steps.say: A stuck bullet ridden out by the next shot puts two bullets through one hole, the tandem bullet puzzle.

nodes.label: Weak first shot lodges in barrel

steps.tx: One skin hole and two projectiles on a chest radiograph point to a **tandem or piggyback bullet**. Faulty ammunition, or a round stored for years amid heat and damp, fires too weakly, so the first bullet stalls inside the barrel. The following shot drives that lodged bullet out ahead of itself, and both pass through the same entrance. Separation may occur within the body or in flight before either reaches the target.
steps.say: One skin hole and two projectiles on a chest radiograph point to a tandem or piggyback bullet. steps.title: Why tandem wounds look long range
steps.tx: Because the second bullet wastes force pushing the first, its energy is directed backward against the obstruction, so **tandem discharge marks are diminished or absent**. Burning, blackening and tattooing fade, and the wound imitates long range fire even at close quarters. The examiner should therefore count bullets on the whole body X ray and compare with entrance wounds before committing to a range opinion in any shooting with an old or neglected weapon.
steps.say: Energy spent pushing the stuck bullet steals the close range marks, so count bullets on X ray before judging range.

steps.title: Souvenir bullets and lead poisoning
steps.tx: A bullet retained for years becomes a **souvenir bullet**, wrapped in a dense fibrous capsule with no fresh bleeding around it and only a small scar marking the original entry. Retained lead is not inert: synovial fluid dissolves lead well, and chronic absorption can produce lead poisoning from a bullet sitting in or near a joint. The capsule and absent haemorrhage separate an old souvenir from a fresh lodged bullet at autopsy.
steps.say: Old retained bullets sit in fibrous capsules without bleeding, and joint fluid dissolving their lead can poison the patient.

steps.title: Dumdum and frangible bullets
steps.tx: A **dumdum bullet** is designed to fragment extensively on striking, and frangible bullets disintegrate almost completely, often into granules that resist recovery even when X ray shows them. They do not ricochet, and matching fragments to a test bullet is difficult or impossible. If bone is penetrated the recovered pieces look eroded. Their wounding comes from many small secondary tracks radiating from the point where the bullet broke apart.
steps.say: Dumdum and frangible bullets shatter into granules that wound widely but leave almost nothing matchable behind.

steps.title: Explosive, incendiary and tracer bullets
steps.tx: Special military bullets add hazards. **Incendiary and explosive bullets** carry phosphorus or an explosive charge that fires on impact, are banned, and make larger wounds with greater fragmentation. Avoid ultrasound and microwave techniques near them, wear goggles, use long handled instruments and store the removed bullet padded against impact, vibration and heat. Tracer bullets merely burn a visible trace in flight so the gunner can follow the shot.
steps.say: Explosive bullets demand forceps, goggles and padded storage, and must never meet ultrasound or microwave energy.

steps.title: Blank cartridges can kill at contact
steps.tx: A **blank cartridge** holds primer, ultrafast powder and wadding but no bullet, yet at close discharge its gases and wadding lacerate tissue and can kill by damaging main vessels or by pressure shock on nerves. Distant blank shots are harmless. Country made and old worn guns add another trap: they can discharge by themselves when dropped on the butt or thrown down, without any finger touching the trigger.
steps.say: A blank fired close can kill with gas and wad alone, and a dropped country gun can fire itself the same way.

steps.title: Bullet embolism, the travelling bullet
steps.tx: A bullet entering a vessel can travel with the blood as a **bullet embolism**. Arterial emboli usually lodge in the femoral and popliteal arteries, while venous emboli, which are less frequent, enter veins of the lower limb or reach the heart. The clue is a bullet on imaging far from any plausible track, or a bullet that moves between two films. Surgical planning must therefore confirm the bullet's position immediately before operation.
steps.say: Bullets can embolise down arteries to leg vessels, so a bullet far from its track needs a fresh film before surgery.

steps.title: Blast injury and blast lung
steps.tx: An explosion throws a concentric pressure wave at about the speed of sound, and above roughly 700 kilopascals it seriously damages the body in **blast injury**. Homogeneous tissues like liver and muscle resist, but air containing lung suffers blast lung: subpleural patchy haemorrhages, alveolar rupture, blood stained froth and later bronchopneumonia. The tympanic membrane ruptures commonly. Death can follow from systemic air embolism entering pulmonary veins through the torn lung.
steps.say: Blast lung tears alveoli and froths the airways, the eardrum bursts early, and air embolism can kill without surface injury.

steps.tx: Skin after an explosion carries a mixed peppering of small bruises, abrasions and puncture lacerations. **Blast injury** begins with a concentric pressure wave travelling near the speed of sound, and pressures above roughly 700 kilopascals seriously damage the body. Solid organs such as liver and muscle resist better than air filled lung, which develops subpleural patchy haemorrhages, alveolar rupture and blood stained froth. The eardrum commonly splits, and air embolism through torn pulmonary veins can kill.

steps.title: The blast triad of flying missiles
steps.tx: Blast drives bomb fragments and nearby gravel, glass, wood and brick into skin as **flying missile injuries**: bruises, abrasions and puncture lacerations intimately mixed, mostly under one centimetre and tending to unite. That mixed triad is diagnostic of explosion. Dust driven in can tattoo the skin fairly uniformly. Falling masonry adds traumatic asphyxia, fumes add carbon monoxide in confined spaces, and X rays hunt the metal of the detonating mechanism inside tissues.
steps.say: Bruise, abrasion and puncture laceration mixed under a centimetre each is the fingerprint of blast driven fragments.
